newsitem.title: GUAM: Investigators eye storm, visibility in KAL crash.
newsitem.headline: Investigators eye storm, visibility in KAL crash.

text.p: Lashing rain and a sudden loss of visibility could have contributed to the crash this week of a Korean Air Lines jumbo jet only a few miles (kilometres) from Guam's main airport, U.S. air crash investigators said on Saturday.

"The immediate question that comes to mind is a combination of a freak, heavy rain shower and destruction of visibility" when the Boeing 747 was making its landing approach, said George Black, leader of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) probe.
He said, however, that this was only one of many possibilities.
On Friday he said no sudden engine failure or major structural accident had occurred. Some media reports said the investigators now were focusing on human error as the cause of the crash.
Korean Air Flight 801, carrying 254 passengers and crew from Seoul to Guam, ploughed into low-lying hills three miles ( five km) from the runway in the early hours of Wednesday.
Only 29 people, including two flight attendants, survived the fiery crash. Most of the passengers were vacationers from South Korea.
Frustrated family members of those presumed dead on Saturday surrounded Korean Air Lines president Cho Yang-ho in a minor scuffle at a on Guam where many of the bereaved relatives are staying.
Cho was not hurt, but three of his bodyguards were pushed and shoved as they tried to protect the airline president. The families have still had no definite word about the fate of their loved ones.

Bus loads of family members were finally allowed to visit the immediate area of the crash site on Saturday, but this still did not prevent them from making frequent verbal outbursts against airline officials for the slow pace of recovery of the bodies.
U.S. officials said they still have not recovered more than half of the bodies and said the poor condition of the remains which had been found was making the body count difficult.
None of the bodies have been identified. To speed up the process, forensics experts started showing photographs of bodies to the family members on Saturday.
Black said the weather and visibility theory was only one of many possibilities after examining preliminary data from the crash site and other records.

But he did say that a weather observer at Guam International Airport told the team that he could not see Nimitz Hills four minutes after the crash, meaning visibility was less than three miles just after the crash, an unusual phenomenon at this airport.

Nimitz Hills is where Flight 801 crashed. Black said this uninhabited area was a dark patch as seen from the sky and said they would try to determine if absence of lights could have contributed to the crash in any way.

Black said it was not clear if the flight crew was making a visual or instrumental approach, although it was cleared for "ILS" or Instrumental Landing System approach. Many pilots use a combination of both methods, which is allowed, he said.
Black said that the NTSB had not determined that human error of some kind was behind the accident.
"We have not found any human error up to this point," Black told a news conference after the second day of the investigation by his 18-member probe team.

On Friday, Black said he found no evidence of mechanical, structural or engine failure. The plane was on a controlled, steady descent towards touchdown. Preliminary evidence also showed, Black said, that the flight crew was unaware of any impending disaster.
Black's team said his team found mud and dirt inside the two engines they examined on Saturday, meaning they were running even after the plane hit the ground.

The crew was aware that a key navigational device at the airport, the glide slope indicator, was not available because of regular maintenance, Black said. His team found further evidence that this was the case on Saturday, a handwritten note of this on a flight crew check sheet.
The NTSB interviewed the flight crew of a Ryan International air cargo flight which landed 30 minutes after Flight 801 was supposed to land.
Black said the first officer of the Ryan plane saw red flashes in hills near the runway which could have been the explosion from the Korean Air flight.
